source.title: RASA: Routing-Aware Safety Alignment for Mixture-of-Experts Models
source.authors: Jiacheng Liang; Yu-Hui Wang; Tan-Qiu Jiang; Ting Wang

page_placements.theme: Mixture-of-experts routing and expert selection mediate safety

record.file_problem: The paper text is present through the appendices. Some table content, especially Table 13, is flattened and difficult to assign; this does not affect the extracted rows.
record.tranche_reason: Tests suffix-based jailbreak success and whether safety behavior is causally concentrated in selected MoE experts, using adaptive attacks and expert parameter interventions rather than the original studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL by response position, compliant-prefix effects, benign fine-tuning, or changes to decoding. Table 4 concerns routing-distribution KL, not token-position KL. Table 5’s explicit GCG-style suffix attack is included for V4; other jailbreak evaluations are not treated as tests of the specific suffix, compliant-opening, or decoding claims. Mechanistic activation and layer-distribution measurements are not rows because they do not themselves measure the behavioral effect named in the versions.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (MoE models), the study reports how often a white-box GCG-style suffix attack (REA) defeats refusal. It does so on the original OLMoE instruct model, a full-parameter safety-tuned version, and the RASA-aligned version. Those rates bear on V4. The other results are about routing shortcuts, and the expert interventions measure safety that RASA itself put into selected experts. Neither matches a version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that full-parameter safety fine-tuning of MoE models can gain safety through routing shortcuts without repairing safety-critical experts. They argue that RASA's targeted expert repair with router consistency gives routing-robust safety: 0.12 ASR under their adaptive attack, with capability preserved. They add that adaptive multi-turn defense remains open.
record.recipe_differences: Uses activation-discrepancy-based expert selection, selective expert fine-tuning under fixed routing, and subsequent router consistency optimization; it does not use the original claims’ general fine-tuning or token-position KL methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by attack and training configuration. The paper reports routing-restoration effects by attack type, differences between single-attack and mixed-attack alignment, and cross-judge differences; REA success also differs across Base, Full-Param FT, and RASA.

fits_no_version.finding: Full-parameter safety fine-tuning of MoE models loses 0.38–0.46 harmlessness when the original prefill routing is forced; RASA loses 0.04–0.06. The text reports a ~0.4 drop on Mixtral too.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE models, safety gains from full-parameter fine-tuning rest largely on changed routing, a shortcut separate from token-position shallowness.

fits_no_version.finding: Restoring the RASA-trained experts drops harmlessness from 1.00 to 0.31, while restoring random experts leaves it at 0.92. Transplanting the repaired experts into the original model raises harmlessness from 0.10 to 0.74.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety injected by selective expert fine-tuning resides mostly in the fine-tuned experts. This is localization imposed by the training design.

record.problems: The paper notes limited adaptive-attack coverage (one GCG-style attack on one architecture), single-LLM-judge evaluation with only subset cross-checking, and evaluation on three open-weight MoE architectures rather than frontier-scale models. It reports no uncertainty estimates for the extracted behavioral results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for the Table 4 routing KL or activation deviations: these are routing measurements, not token-position KL or direct behavioral tests of the versions. Layerwise AAD/SCE counts and attribution overlaps are omitted because they do not independently measure the behavioral outcomes named by the versions. Other attack results are omitted because the text does not establish that they test the specific suffix, compliant-opening, or decoding mechanisms in V4.

untested.parts: No per-token KL by response position; Table 4's KL is over routing distributions.
Compliant-prefix prefilling and decoding changes are not tested. Only one suffix attack is tested, on one architecture, and no no-suffix baseline is given.
The localization of safety in the original or conventionally aligned models is not tested. The expert interventions only probe RASA-injected safety.
RASA does not aim to spread safety beyond the first tokens, and token depth is not measured.

missing.what: Mixtral-8x7B routing-restoration result (Full-Param FT harmlessness drops ~0.4); bears only on the fits_no_version routing finding

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this study. The prompt-rewriting jailbreaks (FlipAttack, DeepInception, Persuasion) are not suffix, prefill or decoding attacks, so they are correctly left out of V4. The record's V5 support is withdrawn: the necessity and sufficiency tests concern experts that RASA itself trained, so they cannot show natural localization of safety. Table 13(d) also reports that random-expert fine-tuning reaches high targeted harmlessness. No uncertainty is reported, and harmlessness is judged by a single LLM judge (GPT-4o-mini).

versions.untested_parts: Does not test harmful-data fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples as a way of removing refusal.
Does not test ordinary or carefully chosen benign-data fine-tuning and harmful compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
Tests one RASA-aware GCG-style suffix attack; does not test compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes.
Causal necessity and sufficiency interventions are reported for OLMoE; the paper does not test low-rank edits or establish the same causal localization on each other architecture.
Does not test whether data or training objectives cause first-token shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate a method intended to spread safety beyond the first response tokens.

rows.subject: OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct (Base, unaligned)
rows.operation_detail: Routing-Evasion Attack (REA), a white-box GCG-style suffix optimizer targeting harmful-request compliance and avoidance of repaired SCEs
rows.note: Base-model comparison for the suffix attack.
rows.check: Table 5 labels the model 'Base (unaligned)', but it is the distributed OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct ('Origin'). That model refuses the anchor prompts, so it is safety-trained. No no-suffix baseline is reported. REA also optimizes for avoiding SCE activation, so it is not a pure GCG attack.

rows.subject: OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct (Full-Param FT)
rows.operation_detail: REA suffix optimizer targets harmful-request compliance and avoidance of repaired SCEs
rows.note: Attack succeeds against Full-Param FT, but less often than against the base model.
rows.check: An ASR of 0.60 means the suffix defeats refusal in most cases, so this is observed, not partial. The lower rate than on the original model reflects the extra safety tuning, not a weaker version of the effect.

rows.subject: OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct (RASA)
rows.operation_detail: REA suffix optimizer targets harmful-request compliance and avoidance of repaired SCEs
rows.note: The paper reports low attack success against RASA in this test.
rows.check: 0.12 ASR is the attack's success against the study's own defense. Keep it as the defended condition, not as evidence about undefended safety-trained models.

source_check.correct: state: partial. REA succeeds at ASR 0.12 against RASA, substantially below 0.85 against the original model and 0.60 against Full-Param FT.
source_check.problem: Nonzero, weakened bypass success supports partial rather than absent; no baseline comparison establishes absence or negligible change.

rows.subject: OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct (RASA-aligned)
rows.operation_detail: Restore AAD-selected Safety-Critical Expert parameters to their original values
rows.note: The authors describe harmlessness as collapsing after restoring the selected experts.
rows.check: Restoring the RASA-trained experts undoes training applied only to those experts, so the collapse is close to built in. It shows where RASA put the safety, not that safety in a safety-trained model is naturally concentrated in few parameters (V5).

rows.subject: OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct (RASA-aligned)
rows.operation_detail: Restore an equal number of randomly chosen expert parameters to original values

conditions.value: equal in number to AAD-selected experts

rows.note: Randomly restoring the same number of experts leaves harmlessness near the RASA-aligned value.
rows.check: The random experts were mostly untrained by RASA, so restoring them is expected to change little. This is not a V5 test.

rows.subject: OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct (Original, unaligned)
rows.operation_detail: Transplant repaired AAD-selected SCEs from RASA into the original model
rows.note: The paper describes the transplanted set as recovering most, but not all, of the safety gain.
rows.check: The transplant moves safety that targeted expert fine-tuning injected. This is localization induced by design, not a measure of how safety is distributed in the original alignment.

rows.subject: OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct (Origin)
rows.operation_detail: Measure harmlessness under the original model’s normal routing as the reference for routing-restoration comparisons
rows.note: This is the reference for a routing-shortcut finding, not a test of the listed versioned claims.
